title: Dissipation-tunable extended and localized steady states in a non-disordered lattice
authors: Ming-Jie Tao, Yi-Ting Wang, Jing Li, Hongsheng Hou, Xiang-Ping Jiang, Lei Pan
abstract: Dissipation is usually regarded as a source of decoherence that suppresses quantum interference and localization. Here we show that suitably engineered dissipation can instead be used to select localized or extended states in a strictly non-disordered one-dimensional lattice. The underlying clean lattice has spatially inhomogeneous hopping and supports both extended bulk states and localized boundary states, including an algebraically localized bound state in the continuum. We introduce a nonlocal bond jump operator with a tunable relative phase and show that this phase selectively favors eigenstates with different spatial phase correlations. As a result, the long-time density matrix can be steered toward sectors dominated by localized or extended Hamiltonian eigenstates without changing any Hamiltonian parameter. The microscopic origin of the selection is quantified by the fraction of site pairs separated by a distance $l$ that are phase matched with the dissipative channel. We further characterize the dissipative quench through the quantum fidelity and show that the selected character of the steady state can persist after the dissipation is removed. Our results establish phase-selective bond dissipation as a route to controllable state preparation and transport manipulation in non-disordered lattices.
summary: This theoretical work shows that controlled dissipation can act as a selective filter, allowing researchers to force a non-disordered quantum lattice into a steady state dominated by either localized or extended wave functions. By tuning the phase of the dissipation, the system's asymptotic state can be controlled without altering the underlying Hamiltonian parameters. This establishes a powerful, dissipation-mediated route for state preparation and transport control.
main_problem: To demonstrate that engineered dissipation can actively select between localized and extended steady states in a strictly non-disordered lattice, challenging the view that dissipation always causes decoherence.
main_result: The system's long-time steady state can be deterministically steered toward sectors dominated by either localized or extended Hamiltonian eigenstates solely by tuning the phase ($\alpha$) of a nonlocal dissipative coupling.
method: The dynamics are analyzed using the Lindblad master equation, casting the evolution into a linear equation on the Liouville-Fock space. State selection is quantified by analyzing the in-phase pair fraction and using quantum fidelity.
model_or_system: The model is a one-dimensional tight-binding lattice with deterministic, inhomogeneous hopping near the boundaries. The dynamics are governed by the Lindblad master equation, incorporating a nonlocal bond jump operator with a tunable relative phase $\alpha$.
key_observables: Participation Ratio (PR), Quantum Fidelity ($F$), and the fraction of in-phase site pairs ($P_{n,l}$).
important_parameters: The relative phase $\alpha$ and the separation distance $l$ of the dissipative coupling are the primary control parameters.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the Born–Markov approximation.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the lattice modulation, the energy spectrum including a Bound State in the Continuum (BIC), and the time evolution of quantum fidelity comparing initial localized vs. extended states under different dissipation phases.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the model, introduces the dissipation mechanism, analyzes the steady-state selection using phase-matching criteria, and confirms the robustness of the prepared state by monitoring quantum fidelity after the quench.
why_interesting: This work provides a concrete, controllable mechanism to manipulate quantum transport and localization in clean systems using engineered dissipation, which is highly relevant for understanding open quantum dynamics in AMO and quantum optics.
